claim: In insects and other arthropods, which have only innate immune mechanisms, four main immune-specific modules have been described in the defense against microbial invaders: the Toll pathway, the Imd pathway, the melanization response, and phagocytosis by plasmatocytes.
source: In insects and other arthropods, which have only innate immune mechanisms, four main immune-specific modules have been described in the defense against microbial invaders: the Toll pathway, the Imd pathway, the melanization response, and phagocytosis by plasmatocytes.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about insect immune systems, drawing from the scientific literature.

claim: Flies simultaneously deficient in all four immune modules are viable (poor viability), homozygous fertile, and display no overt morphological defects.
source: Surprisingly, flies simultaneously deficient in all four immune modules are viable (poor viability), homozygous fertile, and display no overt morphological defects, suggesting these immune mechanisms are not strictly required for organismal development.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental generation of quadruple mutant flies in this study.

claim: These immune mechanisms are not strictly required for organismal development.
source: Surprisingly, flies simultaneously deficient in all four immune modules are viable (poor viability), homozygous fertile, and display no overt morphological defects, suggesting these immune mechanisms are not strictly required for organismal development.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that quadruple mutant flies are viable and fertile.

claim: These four modules largely function independently and additively in host defense.
source: We find these four modules largely function independently and additively in host defense.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from systematic assessment of single and compound mutants across multiple pathogens.

claim: Melanization plays a highly important role against viruses.
source: We also reveal a highly important role of melanization against viruses.
evidence: This is based on survival data showing melanization-deficient flies are susceptible to viral infections.

claim: The Toll pathway is activated by cell wall components (fungal glucans and Lysine-type peptidoglycan), as well as microbial proteases.
source: In Drosophila, the Toll pathway is activated by cell wall components (fungal glucans and Lysine-type peptidoglycan), as well as microbial proteases (Gottar et al., 2006; Issa et al., 2018; Leulier et al., 2003; Vaz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Toll signaling culminates in the activation of two NF-κB transcription factors, Dif and Dorsal, which regulate a large set of immune genes.
source: Toll signaling culminates in the activation of two NF-κB transcription factors, Dif and Dorsal, which regulate a large set of immune genes (Ip, 1993; Lemaitre et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Flies lacking the Toll pathway are viable but highly susceptible to infection by Gram-positive bacteria and fungi.
source: Flies lacking the Toll pathway are viable but highly susceptible to infection by Gram-positive bacteria and fungi (Buchon et al., 2009; Lemaitre et al., 1996; Rutschmann et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Imd pathway is activated by DAP-type peptidoglycan produced by Gram-negative bacteria and a subset of Gram-positive bacteria (e.g. Bacillus).
source: The Imd pathway is activated by DAP-type peptidoglycan produced by Gram-negative bacteria and a subset of Gram-positive bacteria (e.g. Bacillus) (Kaneko et al., 2004; Lemaitre et al., 1995; Leulier et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The binding of peptidoglycan to receptors of the Peptidoglycan Recognition Protein family (PGRP-SD, PGRP-LC, PGRP-LE) initiates an intracellular signaling cascade, which ultimately activates the NF-κB factor Relish.
source: The binding of peptidoglycan to receptors of the Peptidoglycan Recognition Protein family (PGRP-SD, PGRP-LC, PGRP-LE) initiates an intracellular signaling cascade, which ultimately activates the NF-κB factor Relish (Choe et al., 2005; Iatsenko et al., 2016; Kaneko et al., 2006; Westlake et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Imd-deficient flies are viable but susceptible to Gram-negative bacterial infection.
source: Imd-deficient flies are viable but susceptible to Gram-negative bacterial infection.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Imd mutant phenotypes.

claim: Melanization is an arthropod-specific immune response resulting in the rapid deposition of the black pigment melanin at wound or infection sites and the concomitant production of microbicidal reactive oxygen species.
source: Melanization is an arthropod-specific immune response resulting in the rapid deposition of the black pigment melanin at wound or infection sites and the concomitant production of microbicidal reactive oxygen species (Cerenius et al., 2008; Nappi et al., 2009; Westlake et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Two PPOs (PPO1 and PPO2) are the primary catalysts for the synthesis of melanin during the melanization response upon systemic infection.
source: Two PPOs (PPO1 and PPO2) are the primary catalysts for the synthesis of melanin during the melanization response upon systemic infection.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the melanization pathway.

claim: Flies deficient for both PPO1 and PPO2 are viable but lack hemolymph phenoloxidase activity and exhibit susceptibility to certain Gram-positive bacteria and fungi.
source: Flies deficient for both PPO1 and PPO2 are viable but lack hemolymph phenoloxidase activity and exhibit susceptibility to certain Gram-positive bacteria and fungi (Binggeli et al., 2014; Dudzic et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A third PPO gene (PPO3) is specifically expressed by lamellocytes, specialized hemocytes that differentiate in larvae responding to and enveloping invading parasites.
source: In addition, a third PPO gene (PPO3) is specifically expressed by lamellocytes, specialized hemocytes that differentiate in larvae responding to and enveloping invading parasites (Dudzic et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Hemocytes contribute to survival upon systemic infection to certain bacterial species.
source: The use of hemocyte-deficient flies, via the targeted expression of a pro-apoptotic gene in plasmatocytes only, has shown that hemocytes contribute to survival upon systemic infection to certain bacterial species (Charroux and Royet, 2009; Defaye et al., 2009; Stephenson et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Phagocytosis of bacteria greatly relies on two transmembrane receptors, NimC1 and Eater.
source: Phagocytosis of bacteria greatly relies on two transmembrane receptors, NimC1 and Eater (Bretscher et al., 2015; Kocks et al., 2005; Kurucz et al., 2007; Melcarne et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NimC1, Eater double mutant larvae are viable, have elevated hemocyte numbers at the larval stage, and their hemocytes can encapsulate and melanize macroparasites; however, their hemocytes are non-sessile and nearly totally phagocytosis deficient.
source: NimC1, Eater double mutant larvae are viable, have elevated hemocyte numbers at the larval stage, and their hemocytes can encapsulate and melanize macroparasites; however, their hemocytes are non-sessile and nearly totally phagocytosis deficient.
evidence: This is a description of the phenotype of NimC1, Eater mutants from previous studies.

claim: NimC1, Eater adult flies have decreased hemocyte numbers and fail to perform phagocytosis.
source: NimC1, Eater adult flies have decreased hemocyte numbers and fail to perform phagocytosis, providing a good tool to assess the role of the cellular response (Melcarne et al., 2019b; Melcarne, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RelE20, spzrm7 flies were not viable in the DrosDel isogenic background.
source: Of note, in our hands, recombinant RelE20, spzrm7 flies were not viable in the DrosDel isogenic background, forcing us to use non-iso flies to assess the host defense of ΔIMD, ΔTOLL flies.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental work in this study.

claim: NimC11;eater1, spzrm7 flies were not viable.
source: We then generated by recombination six out of the seven combinations of flies simultaneously lacking two immune modules with the exception of ΔTOLL, ΔPhag as NimC11; eater1, spzrm7 flies were not viable (see fly strains in Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental work in this study.

claim: ΔITPM flies (Hayan-pshDef; NimC11; Eater1, RelE20) were homozygous viable with very poor viability and homozygous fertile.
source: Excitingly, we succeeded in generating a fly line deficient for all four immune modules with the genotype: Hayan-pshDef; NimC11; eater1, RelE20 hereafter named ΔITPM (ΔIMD, ΔTOLL, ΔPhag, ΔMel). These flies were homozygous viable with very poor viability and homozygous fertile, despite major deficiencies in these four important systemic immune mechanisms.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental work in this study.

claim: Each of the four immune modules can be selectively blocked in the isogenic DrosDel background without interfering with the competence of the others.
source: Collectively, this analysis indicates that each of the four immune modules can be selectively blocked in the isogenic DrosDel background without interfering with the competence of the others.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the functional assays shown in Figure 1A-D.

claim: The expression level of DptA was roughly similar to the wild-type in ∆TOLL and ∆Mel flies.
source: We note that the expression level of DptA was roughly similar to the wild-type in ∆TOLL and ∆Mel flies; however, DPhag flies show reduced DptA induction at 6 hr compared to WT (~50%) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ΔPhag flies show reduced DptA induction at 6 hr compared to WT (~50%).
source: We note that the expression level of DptA was roughly similar to the wild-type in ∆TOLL and ∆Mel flies; however, DPhag flies show reduced DptA induction at 6 hr compared to WT (~50%) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The Drs induction at 6 hr of ΔMel flies upon heat-killed M. luteus injection was significantly higher than WT (~1.6x).
source: On the other hand, the Drs induction at 6 hr of DMel flies upon heat-killed M. luteus injection was significantly higher than WT (~1.6x), as found previously using live M. luteus infection (Binggeli et al., 2014; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 1B and is consistent with a previous study.

claim: ∆IMD and ∆Mel mutant larvae had similar levels of phagocytic index to the wild-type.
source: Furthermore, ∆IMD and ∆Mel mutant larvae had similar levels of phagocytic index to the wild-type (Figure 1C), while ∆TOLL had a higher phagocytic index, if anything.
evidence: This is based on ex vivo phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ∆TOLL had a higher phagocytic index compared to wild-type.
source: Furthermore, ∆IMD and ∆Mel mutant larvae had similar levels of phagocytic index to the wild-type (Figure 1C), while ∆TOLL had a higher phagocytic index, if anything.
evidence: This is based on ex vivo phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There was no apparent melanization at the site of the injury in ∆Mel flies.
source: As expected, there was no apparent melanization at the site of the injury in ∆Mel flies, while melanization blackening was readily observed in the wild-type and in other single-module mutants (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on visual observation of melanization after injury shown in Figure 1D.

claim: ΔITPM flies, although viable, are indeed fully immune deficient for the four host defense modules.
source: Not surprisingly, all compound flies display the expected immune deficiencies validating the lines we constructed. This analysis confirms that ΔITPM flies, although viable, are indeed fully immune deficient for the four host defense modules.
evidence: This is based on the functional assays shown in Figure 1E-H.

claim: A small level of Drs expression is retained in ∆TOLL mutant flies but was fully abolished in ∆IMD, ∆TOLL flies.
source: Notably, a small level of Drs expression is retained in ∆TOLL mutant flies but was fully abolished in ∆IMD, ∆TOLL flies (Figure 1A and E), confirming the Drs gene receives a small input from the Imd pathway (Leulier et al., 2000).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 1A and E, and is consistent with a previous study.

claim: The Drs gene receives a small input from the Imd pathway.
source: Notably, a small level of Drs expression is retained in ∆TOLL mutant flies but was fully abolished in ∆IMD, ∆TOLL flies (Figure 1A and E), confirming the Drs gene receives a small input from the Imd pathway (Leulier et al., 2000).
evidence: This is confirmed by the data in this study and supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: At 25°C, no single mutants died significantly more than the wild-type in the absence of challenge within the 10-day window.
source: At 25°C, no single mutants died significantly more than the wild-type in the absence of challenge within the 10-day window (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Each compound mutant other than ∆IMD, ΔTOLL suffered 25% cumulative mortality by 10 days post-eclosion at 25°C.
source: However, looking at compound mutants, even in the absence of challenge, each compound mutant other than ∆IMD, ΔTOLL suffered 25% cumulative mortality by 10 days post-eclosion, while ∆TOLL, ΔMelPPS, and ∆ITPM flies suffered even greater cumulative mortality.
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ∆TOLL, ΔMelPPS, and ∆ITPM flies suffered even greater cumulative mortality than other compound mutants at 25°C.
source: However, looking at compound mutants, even in the absence of challenge, each compound mutant other than ∆IMD, ΔTOLL suffered 25% cumulative mortality by 10 days post-eclosion, while ∆TOLL, ΔMelPPS, and ∆ITPM flies suffered even greater cumulative mortality.
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ΔITPM flies have the lowest unchallenged survival rate of genotypes included in this study.
source: ΔITPM flies (Hayan-pshDef; NimC11; Eater1, RelE20) have the lowest unchallenged survival rate of genotypes included in this study.
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Imd, Toll, Melanization, and Phagocytosis modules contribute little to lifespan maintenance individually, but are crucial to maintain lifespan collectively.
source: Taken together, the Imd, Toll, Melanization, and Phagocytosis modules contribute little to lifespan maintenance individually, but are crucial to maintain lifespan collectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is inferred from the survival data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: ∆Mel flies showed a cumulative mortality of ~50% by day 10 after clean injury.
source: We found a cumulative mortality of ~50% for ∆Mel flies by day 10 (Figure 2C), while other single-module mutants displayed relatively little mortality over the 10-day window.
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: All the compound mutants affected in melanization were susceptible to clean injury.
source: Consistent with an importance of melanization in the injury response (Binggeli et al., 2014), all the compound mutants affected in melanization were susceptible to clean injury, with similar mortality seen in ΔPhag, ΔMel, ΔIMD, ΔMel, ΔTOLL, ΔMelPPS, ΔTOLL, ΔMelHP, and ΔITPM flies (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 2D and is consistent with a previous study.

claim: All these immune modules contribute somewhat to the survival of flies upon clean injury, with a major role of the melanization response in maintaining lifespan and survival to injury.
source: Collectively, our study highlights that all these immune modules contribute somewhat to the survival of flies upon clean injury, with a major role of the melanization response in maintaining lifespan and survival to injury.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the survival data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The Imd pathway plays a major role against all tested Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Our study confirms that the Imd pathway plays a major role against all tested Gram-negative bacteria, as ∆IMD flies succumb more rapidly than wild-type flies to all of them.
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 3 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The Imd pathway contributes to survival against the Gram-positive bacteria B. subtilis and L. monocytogenes.
source: This pathway also contributes, albeit to a lesser extent, to survival against the Gram-positive bacteria B. subtilis and L. monocytogenes, which bear DAP-type peptidoglycan at their membrane that triggers Imd activation (Kaneko et al., 2004; Leulier et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 3 and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: ∆IMD mutant flies were somewhat susceptible to the four viruses DCV, FHV, DXV, and IIV6, but not SINV.
source: We found that ∆IMD mutant flies were somewhat susceptible to the four viruses DCV, FHV, DXV, and IIV6, but not SINV, agreeing with previous studies showing a reduction in lifespan of 1–2 days for Rel mutant flies after viral infection (Costa et al., 2009; Goto et al., 2018; Sansone et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 3 and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: The Toll pathway plays a prominent role in survival upon infection by all virulent Gram-positive bacteria and fungi upon septic injury.
source: This study also confirms a prominent role of the Toll pathway in survival upon infection by all virulent Gram-positive bacteria and fungi upon septic injury.
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 3 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: ΔTOLL flies show susceptibility to FHV, DXV, and IIV6.
source: In addition, we found a susceptibility of ΔTOLL flies to FHV, DXV, and IIV6, suggesting Toll-regulated effectors mediate defense against viral infection.
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Toll-regulated effectors mediate defense against viral infection.
source: In addition, we found a susceptibility of ΔTOLL flies to FHV, DXV, and IIV6, suggesting Toll-regulated effectors mediate defense against viral infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the susceptibility of ΔTOLL flies to certain viruses.

claim: ΔPhag mutants reveal a role of the cellular response in survival against the fungus B. bassiana.
source: Use of DPhag mutants reveals a role of the cellular response in survival against the fungus B. bassiana.
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 3.

claim: ΔPhag flies show a minor susceptibility to S. aureus and a subset of Gram-negative bacteria (Pr. rettgeri, Ecc15, and E. coli).
source: DPhag flies further show a minor susceptibility to S. aureus and a subset of Gram-negative bacteria (Pr. rettgeri, Ecc15, and E. coli).
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Melanization plays a relatively consistent role against all the tested viruses, notably so for DXV, IIV-6, and SINV.
source: Surprisingly, our study reveals a relatively consistent role of melanization against all the tested viruses, notably so for DXV, IIV-6, and SINV.
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 3.

claim: ∆Mel flies display a minor increased susceptibility to B. bassiana natural infection and septic injury.
source: ∆Mel flies also display a minor increased susceptibility to B. bassiana natural infection and septic injury.
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 3.

claim: ΔMel flies are highly susceptible to the Gram-positive bacterium S. aureus, rivaling the susceptibility of ΔITPM flies.
source: As previously described (Dudzic et al., 2019), DMel flies are highly susceptible to the Gram-positive bacterium S. aureus, rivaling the susceptibility of DITPM flies.
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 3 and is consistent with a previous study.

claim: ΔMel flies show a strong susceptibility to Pr. rettgeri rivaling ΔIMD flies.
source: DMel flies further show a strong susceptibility to Pr. rettgeri rivaling DIMD flies, and also a minor susceptibility to infection by other Gram-negative bacteria (Pr. burhodogranariea, E. coli).
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 3.

claim: AMPs are critical for survival to infection against all Gram-negative bacteria tested.
source: Here we found that AMPs are critical for survival to infection against all Gram-negative bacteria tested, often rivaling the susceptibility of DIMD flies.
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 3.

claim: ΔAMP14 flies were somewhat susceptible to the yeast C. albicans and the Gram-positive bacteria B. subtilis and M. luteus.
source: Notably, DAMP14 flies were also somewhat susceptible to the yeast C. albicans and the Gram-positive bacteria B. subtilis and M. luteus, reinforcing minor susceptibilities seen previously (Carboni et al., 2022; Hanson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 3 and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: ΔAMP14 survivals to DCV, FHV, DXV, and IIV6 largely paralleled those of ΔIMD flies.
source: Interestingly, we found that DAMP14 survivals to DCV, FHV, DXV, and IIV6 largely paralleled those of DIMD flies (Figure 3, Supplementary file 1), suggesting Imd-mediated survival phenotypes rely greatly on the presence of the seven classical AMP families.
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Imd-mediated survival phenotypes rely greatly on the presence of the seven classical AMP families.
source: Interestingly, we found that DAMP14 survivals to DCV, FHV, DXV, and IIV6 largely paralleled those of DIMD flies (Figure 3, Supplementary file 1), suggesting Imd-mediated survival phenotypes rely greatly on the presence of the seven classical AMP families.
evidence: This is inferred from the parallel susceptibilities of ΔAMP14 and ΔIMD flies to viruses.

claim: ΔBom flies were susceptible to septic injury by B. bassiana and also somewhat to C. albicans.
source: On the other hand, DBom flies were susceptible to septic injury by B. bassiana and also somewhat to C. albicans, consistent with previous studies (Supplementary file 2), as well as all virulent Gram-positive bacteria, consistent with their important role downstream of the Toll pathway (Clemmons et al., 2015; Lindsay et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on survival data and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: ΔBom flies were susceptible to all virulent Gram-positive bacteria.
source: On the other hand, DBom flies were susceptible to septic injury by B. bassiana and also somewhat to C. albicans, consistent with previous studies (Supplementary file 2), as well as all virulent Gram-positive bacteria, consistent with their important role downstream of the Toll pathway (Clemmons et al., 2015; Lindsay et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on survival data and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: ΔBom flies paralleled the ΔTOLL susceptibility to DCV, FHV, and DXV, but were not susceptible to IIV6 like ΔTOLL.
source: In addition, DBom flies paralleled the DTOLL susceptibility to DCV, FHV, and DXV, but were not susceptible to IIV6 like DTOLL.
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 3.

claim: AMPs play a key role downstream of the Imd pathway in the defense against Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Collectively, our study confirms the key role of AMPs downstream of the Imd pathway in the defense against Gram-negative bacteria, and a primary role of Bomanins downstream of Toll in defense against fungi and Gram-positive bacteria, with little input to survival against Gram-negative bacteria.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the survival data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Bomanins play a primary role downstream of Toll in defense against fungi and Gram-positive bacteria, with little input to survival against Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Collectively, our study confirms the key role of AMPs downstream of the Imd pathway in the defense against Gram-negative bacteria, and a primary role of Bomanins downstream of Toll in defense against fungi and Gram-positive bacteria, with little input to survival against Gram-negative bacteria.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the survival data shown in Figure 3.

claim: AMPs and Bomanins can contribute to survival after certain viral infections.
source: We additionally find these secreted peptides can contribute to survival after certain viral infections.
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 3.

claim: ΔITPM flies, which lack the four modules, were always as or more susceptible than single- and double-module-deficient flies.
source: We first observed that ΔITPM flies, which lack the four modules, were always as or more susceptible than single- and double-module-deficient flies.
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 3.

claim: ΔIMD, ΔTOLL deletion causes complete ΔITPM-like susceptibility to B. subtilis, M. luteus, and E. coli, and near-complete susceptibility to Sa. typhimurium.
source: For instance, ΔIMD, ΔTOLL deletion causes complete DITPM-like susceptibility to B. subtilis, M. luteus, and E. coli, and near-complete susceptibility to Sa. typhimurium.
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 3.

claim: ΔIMD, ΔTOLL causes increased susceptibility to most viruses compared to their individual mutant strains.
source: ΔIMD, ΔTOLL further causes increased susceptibility to most viruses compared to their individual mutant strains.
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 3.

claim: ΔTOLL, ΔMelPPS tended to succumb to infection to a greater extent than ΔTOLL, ΔMelHP.
source: We also observed intriguing differences between our two versions of ΔTOLL, ΔMel flies, as ΔTOLL, ΔMelPPS tended to succumb to infection to a greater extent than ΔTOLL, ΔMelHP, consistent with the differences observed upon clean injury (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 2.

claim: Use of double-module-deficient flies uncovers the role of immune modules to host defense that were masked by other modules.
source: Collectively, use of double-module-deficient flies uncovers the role of immune modules to host defense that were masked by other modules.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the survival data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Most modules contribute to defense independently.
source: While DIMD and ΔTOLL deficiencies sometimes displayed a synergistic effect (i.e. little mortality of single mutants, but DITPM-like mortality of double mutants), for combinations of other pathways, the results were more often minor with a cumulative effect on susceptibility, suggesting most modules contribute to defense independently.
evidence: This is inferred from the survival data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Flies singly deficient for IMD, Phagocytosis, or Melanization modules display a higher bacterial load than wild-type when infected with Pr. rettgeri.
source: Agreeing with contributions to survival, flies singly deficient for IMD, Phagocytosis, or Melanization modules display a higher bacterial load than wild-type when infected with Pr. rettgeri (Figure 4A), which was apparent after 12 hr post-infection.
evidence: This is based on microbial load data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ΔIMD flies, ΔMel flies, and ΔITPM flies that each succumb completely to Pr. rettgeri infection show high and consistent microbe loads at 24 hr indicative of all individuals progressing toward sepsis-induced death.
source: We observed that DIMD flies, DMel flies, and DITPM flies that each succumb completely to Pr. rettgeri infection also show high and consistent microbe loads at 24 hr indicative of all individuals progressing toward sepsis-induced death.
evidence: This is based on microbial load data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Wild-type, ΔTOLL, and ΔPhag flies show a greater stochasticity in bacterial load at 24 hr after Pr. rettgeri infection, consistent with a fraction of individuals surviving the infection by controlling the pathogen.
source: On the other hand, wild-type, DTOLL, and DPhag flies show a greater stochasticity in bacterial load at 24 hr, consistent with a fraction of individuals surviving the infection by controlling the pathogen.
evidence: This is based on microbial load data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Deletion of the Toll pathway and phagocytosis does not fully ablate essential resistance mechanisms for combatting Pr. rettgeri.
source: This indicates deletion of the Toll pathway, and phagocytosis does not fully ablate essential resistance mechanisms for combatting Pr. rettgeri.
evidence: This is inferred from the stochasticity in bacterial loads and survival of some individuals in these genotypes.

claim: Some individuals with higher bacterial loads were observed in ∆Phag and ∆IMD flies at 2 and 6 hr after S. aureus infection, which was not seen in wild-type, ∆TOLL, or ∆Mel flies.
source: In the case of S. aureus (Figure 4B), we observed some individuals with higher bacterial loads in ∆Phag and ∆IMD flies at 2 and 6 hr, which was not seen in wild-type, ∆TOLL, or ∆Mel flies.
evidence: This is based on microbial load data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The Imd pathway can suppress early S. aureus growth.
source: This suggests the Imd pathway can suppress early S. aureus growth, and possibly also phagocytosis, although this ∆Phag could ultimately stem from lesser Imd induction.
evidence: This is inferred from the higher bacterial loads in ∆IMD and ∆Phag flies at early time points.

claim: Flies lacking melanization displayed the highest susceptibility to S. aureus but did not depart from wild-type or other modules in pathogen load until 12 hr post-infection.
source: Interestingly, flies lacking melanization displayed the highest susceptibility but did not depart from wild-type or other modules in pathogen load until 12 hr post-infection.
evidence: This is based on microbial load data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The killing activity of the melanization response acts with slower kinetics against S. aureus.
source: While the melanization reaction is a rapid response, these results suggest that the killing activity of the melanization response acts with slower kinetics.
evidence: This is inferred from the delayed increase in S. aureus loads in ΔMel flies.

claim: ΔITPM flies succumb even more quickly than individual modules to S. aureus due to loss of multiple resistance mechanisms with different kinetics of activation that independently contribute to defense.
source: These trends agree both with survival data kinetics and an independent action of each of these pathways in their resistance effects against S. aureus. This suggests that DITPM flies succumb even more quickly than individual modules due to loss of multiple resistance mechanisms with different kinetics of activation that independently contribute to defense.
evidence: This is inferred from the microbial load and survival data for S. aureus.

claim: ∆TOLL already shows high C. albicans loads at 24 hr.
source: In microbial growth kinetics, ∆TOLL already shows high C. albicans loads at 24 hr consistent with a previous study (Hanson et al., 2019) and observations done with Candida glabrata (Quintin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on microbial load data shown in Figure 4C and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: A few ∆IMD flies showed elevated growth of C. albicans at early time points.
source: Interestingly, a few ∆IMD flies also showed elevated growth of C. albicans at early time points.
evidence: This is based on microbial load data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Imd-regulated effectors could help to suppress initial C. albicans growth.
source: This suggests Imd-regulated effectors could help to suppress initial C. albicans growth, while Toll-regulated genes (e.g. Bomanins, Drs) contribute to this pathogen suppression to a greater extent at later time points.
evidence: This is inferred from the elevated C. albicans growth in some ∆IMD flies at early time points.

claim: Toll-regulated genes (e.g. Bomanins, Drs) contribute to C. albicans pathogen suppression to a greater extent at later time points.
source: This suggests Imd-regulated effectors could help to suppress initial C. albicans growth, while Toll-regulated genes (e.g. Bomanins, Drs) contribute to this pathogen suppression to a greater extent at later time points.
evidence: This is inferred from the high C. albicans loads in ∆TOLL flies at 24 hr.

claim: ∆Phag and ∆Mel flies did not show any increased C. albicans loads within the 24 hr time window despite onset of mortality at later time points.
source: On the other hand, ∆Phag and ∆Mel flies did not show any increased C. albicans loads within the 24 hr time window despite onset of mortality at later time points.
evidence: This is based on microbial load data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ∆ITPM flies displayed more consistent and rapid growth of C. albicans than ΔTOLL or ΔIMD alone, particularly visible at 12–24 hr post-infection.
source: Finally, ∆ITPM flies displayed more consistent and rapid growth of C. albicans than DTOLL or DIMD alone, particularly visible at 12–24 hr post-infection, consistent with independent contributions of both Toll and Imd in resistance to this yeast.
evidence: This is based on microbial load data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Both Toll and Imd independently contribute to resistance against C. albicans.
source: Finally, ∆ITPM flies displayed more consistent and rapid growth of C. albicans than DTOLL or DIMD alone, particularly visible at 12–24 hr post-infection, consistent with independent contributions of both Toll and Imd in resistance to this yeast.
evidence: This is inferred from the more rapid C. albicans growth in ∆ITPM flies compared to single mutants.

claim: For all three pathogens (Pr. rettgeri, S. aureus, and C. albicans), the rank order of susceptibility was broadly similar between males and females, with higher rates of mortality in females overall.
source: For all three pathogens (Pr. rettgeri, S. aureus, and C. albicans), the rank order of susceptibility was broadly similar between males and females, with higher rates of mortality in females overall.
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no marked sex-by-genotype interaction in susceptibility to Pr. rettgeri, S. aureus, and C. albicans.
source: Thus, we found no marked sex-by-genotype interaction.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar rank order of susceptibility between males and females.

claim: The sexual dimorphism in defense against infection is due to factors independent of the immune modules disrupted in this study.
source: However, these data may suggest the sexual dimorphism in defense against infection that we see against these pathogens is due to factors independent of the immune modules we disrupted.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that females are more susceptible even in ∆ITPM flies.

claim: Microbial growth parallels the susceptibility of modules indicating that they work in resistance.
source: Collectively, we observed that microbial growth parallels the susceptibility of modules indicating that they work in resistance.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the microbial load data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The PLUD of both Pr. rettgeri and S. aureus upon death was overall similar in wild-type and single-module mutant flies.
source: The PLUD of both Pr. rettgeri and S. aureus upon death was overall similar in wild-type and single-module mutant flies (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is based on PLUD data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: The distribution of PLUD values for ΔPhag flies infected with C. albicans was markedly different from wild-type.
source: For C. albicans, the distribution of PLUD values for DPhag flies was markedly different from wild-type, also seen to some extent for DMel.
evidence: This is based on PLUD data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The humoral immune pathways, particularly Toll, contribute to resistance against C. albicans.
source: Taken together, this suggests that the humoral immune pathways, particularly Toll, contribute to resistance against C. albicans.
evidence: This is inferred from the high C. albicans loads in ∆TOLL flies and the PLUD data.

claim: The cellular response and melanization reaction regulate tolerance to C. albicans infection.
source: However, the cellular response and melanization reaction instead regulate tolerance to C. albicans infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the lower PLUD in ΔPhag and ΔMel flies despite their ability to suppress C. albicans growth.

claim: When both resistance (Toll, Imd) and tolerance (Phagocytosis, Melanization) mechanisms are deficient, the loss of resistance plays primary importance and can mask the loss of tolerance from being observed.
source: The use of ∆ITPM flies further emphasizes that when both resistance (Toll, Imd) and tolerance (Phagocytosis, Melanization) mechanisms are deficient, the loss of resistance plays primary importance and can mask the loss of tolerance from being observed.
evidence: This is inferred from the PLUD data for ∆ITPM flies.

claim: Some modules, specifically phagocytosis and melanization, contribute to tolerance of certain infections.
source: Collectively, monitoring of PLUD suggests that some modules, specifically phagocytosis and melanization, contribute to tolerance of certain infections.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the PLUD data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The tolerance effect of phagocytosis and melanization was only seen in genotypes that can resist infection.
source: Importantly, this tolerance effect was only seen in genotypes that can resist infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that tolerance effects are masked in ∆ITPM flies.

claim: A higher Toll activation in ∆Mel flies upon systemic infection with dead bacteria was observed.
source: We did, however, observe a higher Toll activation in ∆Mel flies upon systemic infection with dead bacteria.
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A lesser Imd activation in ∆Phag flies at 6 hr post-infection was observed.
source: We also observed a lesser Imd activation in ∆Phag flies at 6 hr post-infection, which could reflect a role for hemocytes to stimulate the Imd systemic response.
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Hemocytes may play a role in stimulating the Imd systemic response.
source: We also observed a lesser Imd activation in ∆Phag flies at 6 hr post-infection, which could reflect a role for hemocytes to stimulate the Imd systemic response.
evidence: This is speculated based on the lesser Imd activation in ∆Phag flies.

claim: NimC11; eater1 double mutants have defects in phagocytosis, but also adhesion and sessility.
source: In this study, we used NimC11; eater1 double mutants to assess the cellular response. These flies have defects in phagocytosis, but also adhesion and sessility (Melcarne et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: NimC11; eater1 larvae have increased hemocyte number at the larval stage, but adults rapidly lose Hml-positive cells.
source: NimC11; eater1 larvae also have increased hemocyte number at the larval stage, but adults rapidly lose Hml-positive cells (Melcarne, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: ∆ITPM flies are almost completely immune deficient, but they can still clot wounds, activate the JNK and JAK–STAT pathways that mediate the wound healing response, and retain constitutive immune defense molecules.
source: Theoretically, ∆ITPM flies are almost completely immune deficient, but they can still clot wounds, activate the JNK and JAK–STAT pathways that mediate the wound healing response, and retain constitutive immune defense molecules that could also provide a certain degree of protection.
evidence: This is inferred from the known functions of immune pathways not disrupted in ∆ITPM flies.

claim: Toll and melanization synergistically contribute to wound healing in adults.
source: Consistent with several studies (Capilla et al., 2017; Carvalho et al., 2014; Rämet et al., 2002), we show that Toll and melanization synergistically contribute to wound healing in adults.
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 2 and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: The Imd pathway and phagocytosis also contribute to wound healing.
source: However, the observation that ∆Phag, ∆Mel or ∆IMD, ∆Mel double mutant flies are also more susceptible to clean injury than ∆Mel flies indicates that the Imd pathway and phagocytosis also contribute to wound healing.
evidence: This is inferred from the survival data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Although immune-deficient fly lines for the four modules are viable, the use of compound mutation and ∆ITPM flies reveals a clear role of the immune system in response to wounding and lifespan maintenance.
source: Thus, although immune-deficient fly lines for the four modules are viable, the use of compound mutation and ∆ITPM flies reveals a clear role of the immune system in response to wounding and lifespan maintenance.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the survival data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Bomanin effectors explain most of the Toll contribution upon septic injury but not natural infection for B. bassiana.
source: However, our study reveals that Bomanin effectors explain most of the Toll contribution upon septic injury but not natural infection, for B. bassiana.
evidence: This is based on survival data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Different importance of effectors or modules occurs according to the route of infection.
source: This observation is in line with different importance of effectors or modules according to the route of infection (Martins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Many immune-inducible regulated genes receive input from both the Imd and Toll pathways, including genes like Metchnikowin, Drosomycin, and Transferrin1.
source: Synergy between Toll and Imd can be explained by the fact that many immune-inducible regulated genes receive input from both the Imd and Toll pathways, including genes like Metchnikowin, Drosomycin, and Transferrin1 (De Gregorio et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Phagocytes or melanization are critical to handle bacteria that resist HDPs or can hide from them.
source: We speculate that phagocytes or melanization are critical to handle bacteria that resist HDPs (Hanson et al., 2019), or can hide from them (Touré et al., 2023).
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed susceptibilities and supported by citations.

claim: The melanization reaction is a source of ROS that is potent against pathogens such as S. aureus that have been shown to be sensitive to ROS and resistant to Toll and Imd defenses.
source: The melanization reaction is a source of ROS that is potent against pathogens such as S. aureus that have been shown to be sensitive to ROS and resistant to Toll and Imd defenses (Dudzic et al., 2019; Ford and King, 2021; Needham et al., 2004; Ramond et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pathogens that have intermediate levels of virulence, killing only a fraction of wild-type flies, may better reveal the role of multiple modules.
source: We hypothesize that pathogens that have intermediate levels of virulence, killing only a fraction of wild-type flies, may better reveal the role of multiple modules.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that multiple modules are important for intermediate virulence pathogens.

claim: The stochasticity in survival analysis partly stems from the arms race occurring between the pathogen and host immunity.
source: Indeed, the stochasticity in survival analysis partly stems from the arms race occurring between the pathogen and host immunity, as shown for Pr. rettgeri (Duneau et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Any small change in the immune system may tip the outcome of the arms race toward lethality or survival for pathogens with intermediate virulence.
source: In this condition, any small change in the immune system may tip the outcome of the arm race toward lethality or survival.
evidence: This is inferred from the stochasticity observed in survival to intermediate virulence pathogens.

claim: A previous study showed a major role of the Imd pathway-regulated AMP Diptericin A against Pr. rettgeri.
source: Previous studies have revealed a major role of the Imd pathway-regulated AMP Diptericin A against this bacterium (Hanson et al., 2023; Hanson et al., 2019; Unckless et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Survival patterns to Pr. rettgeri bifurcate into two outcomes based on time taken to fully activate systemic defenses.
source: However, Duneau et al. showed that survival patterns to Pr. rettgeri bifurcate into two outcomes based on time taken to fully activate systemic defenses (Duneau et al., 2017a), and showed a role for a Toll-PO SP cascade regulating serine protease in defense against this microbe (Duneau et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A Toll-PO SP cascade regulating serine protease plays a role in defense against Pr. rettgeri.
source: However, Duneau et al. showed that survival patterns to Pr. rettgeri bifurcate into two outcomes based on time taken to fully activate systemic defenses (Duneau et al., 2017a), and showed a role for a Toll-PO SP cascade regulating serine protease in defense against this microbe (Duneau et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Susceptibility to fungal infection independent of fungal proliferation has been reported using an A. fumigatus septic infection model and relies on the protection offered by Bomanins from pathogen-secreted toxins.
source: Susceptibility to fungal infection independent of fungal proliferation has also been reported using an A. fumigatus septic infection model and relies on the protection offered by Bomanins from pathogen-secreted toxins (Xu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The loss of tolerance to C. albicans observed may be related to wound repair or accumulating damage, such as renal failure in beetles or autotoxic trachea degradation in flies.
source: It is tempting to speculate, based on the modules involved, that the loss of tolerance to C. albicans we observe has to do with wound repair or accumulating damage, such as what has been reported in beetles that suffer renal failure (Khan et al., 2017; Li et al., 2020), or flies with autotoxic trachea degradation upon stress pathway disruption (Rommelaere et al., 2024).
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed phenotypes and supported by citations.
